title: Low pressure, slow pulse, warm skin
objective: Recognize neurogenic shock -- hypotension with bradycardia after spinal cord injury

brief.situation: 16:20 in the emergency department trauma bay. You are the trauma nurse. Mr. Osei, 23, dove into a shallow lake and didn't come up; friends pulled him out. EMS brings him in a cervical collar with blocks on a board.
handover: EMS: 'Couldn't move his legs at the scene. Pressure's been in the 80s the whole way, pulse in the 50s.' Two IVs in, 500 mL crystalloid given.

The trauma team's orders so far: spinal motion restriction, crystalloid boluses for hypotension, trauma labs and type and screen, CT when stable enough. The trauma physician is at the head of the bed and wants your findings.
Unit practice: a vasopressor runs only on the physician's order, to the MAP target the physician sets.
howItWorks: The clock runs in simulated time; study pace runs three simulated minutes per real minute. Pause any time.
Each assessment takes the time on its button. Decide what the pattern means, what to rule out and what to tell the physician.
Partway through you are asked to write what you think is happening. A debrief scores what you did.

then.log: Talking in full sentences. Belly rises more than the chest with each breath; SpO2 {spo2}%.
No external bleeding; abdomen soft; pelvis stable; thighs normal. Bedside ultrasound: no free fluid. Hemoglobin 14.1 g/dL.
Warm, dry and pink to the toes, capillary refill 2 seconds, despite a blood pressure of {sbp}/{dbp}.
Shrugs and bends his elbows; no grip, nothing below. Sensation lost from the nipple line down. A cervical cord injury.

why.question: Why is Mr. Osei's pressure low, and what does he need?

parts.label: Which shock
parts.criteria: Hypotension with bradycardia and warm, dry skin after a cervical cord injury is neurogenic shock (lost sympathetic tone), but in trauma it is a diagnosis of exclusion: bleeding is looked for first and not found.
parts.modelAnswer: A low pressure with a slow pulse and warm, pink skin after a cord injury at the neck is neurogenic shock, not the cold, fast picture of bleeding. In trauma I still rule out bleeding first: chest, abdomen, pelvis and long bones are clear.

parts.label: What he needs
parts.criteria: Crystalloid first, but fluid alone will not restore the tone: report to the physician for a vasopressor to a MAP target (85 or more); keep the collar and motion restriction; atropine for symptomatic bradycardia.
parts.modelAnswer: A fluid bolus first, then tell the physician that fluid isn't enough: he needs a vasopressor to a MAP of 85 or more, and atropine ready for the slow heart rate. The collar stays on.

noProgress.rationale: An hour of unsupported hypotension after a cord injury risks secondary injury to the cord, which is harm here.

expertPath.text: Collar stays on. Breathing: diaphragmatic but adequate. A crystalloid bolus.
Bleeding screen: chest, abdomen, pelvis, long bones and ultrasound all clear.
Warm pink skin, heart rate 52, a sensory level at the nipples: neurogenic shock.
Report to the physician; start the vasopressor to a MAP of 85 or more; hand off for CT and the ICU.

moved.headline: The neck moved
moved.body: An unstable cervical injury stays in its collar and blocks until imaging and the team clear it.

ischemia.headline: Prolonged hypotension
ischemia.body: Fluid first, but neurogenic shock is lost vascular tone: fluid alone won't fix it. Once bleeding is ruled out, ask for a vasopressor to a MAP target.

supported.headline: Recognized and supported
supported.body: You ruled out bleeding, gave fluid, read the slow pulse and warm skin as neurogenic shock and got a vasopressor running within minutes, collar on. That is the expert path.

slower.headline: Supported, with delays
slower.body: Check whether bleeding was ruled out first, whether fluid came before the pressor, and how long the MAP sat below 80.

time_up.headline: Still hypotensive
time_up.body: Neurogenic shock needs a vasopressor within minutes of being recognized.

scoring.modelReasoning: After a diving injury with a cervical cord level, hypotension with a slow pulse and warm, pink skin is neurogenic shock: the cord injury has cut the sympathetic tone. In trauma it is a diagnosis of exclusion, so bleeding is looked for first and not found. Crystalloid comes first, but fluid alone won't restore the tone: the physician orders a vasopressor to a MAP of 85 or more and atropine for symptomatic bradycardia. The collar stays on throughout.

fluidQ.ask: While he goes to CT: why did he need a vasopressor after fluid?

choices.label: Fluid alone doesn't restore the vascular tone the cord injury removed

fluidQ.explain: IV fluids are not adequate for hypotension caused by neurogenic shock; these patients need vasopressors.
